study.title: 2 Chronicles 35 The Passover of Josiah, its fall and its legacy
study.overview: The chapter presents Josiah as a king who reforms the worship, organizes priests and Levites, and celebrates a large-scale passover in Jerusalem with fidelity to the law of Moses. The account highlights the cooperation between king, leaders, priests, Levites and people, showing order, generosity, and obedience. Then the text changes tone and narrates the reckless decision of Josiah to confront Necho, his deadly wound in Megiddo, the mourning of Judah and the honorable memory preserved about his life. The chapter ends by remembering that the acts of Josiah are recorded in other real sources.

outline.title: Preparation of the easter and reorganization of the cult
outline.explanation: Josiah establishes the celebration of the Passover, confirms the priests in their shifts and guides the Levites to place the ark in the temple, resuming the order of worship according to the law of Moses and the models of David and Solomon. The focus is on holiness, organization and liturgical obedience.

outline.title: The King's Generosity and the Execution of the Sacrifice
outline.explanation: The king and his officers provide beasts in abundance for the Passover. Priests and Levites fulfill distinct functions, blood is manipulated by the priests, the Levites assist in preparing, and the people readily receive the food of the sacrifice, showing a well-coordinated cult.

outline.title: Ordained Praise and an unprecedented easter
outline.explanation: Singers and porters remain in their posts, the Levites meet practical needs and the entire ceremony is completed on the same day, followed by the feast of unleavened breads for seven days. The text states that there has been no similar easter since Samuel's days and places the event in the eighteenth year of Josiah.

outline.title: The death of Josiah, the mourning and the final memory
outline.explanation: After the reform, Josiah confronts Neco and rejects the warning received through him, resulting in his death in Megiddo. Judah and Jerusalem mourn the king, Jeremiah composed lamentations for him, and the chapter closes pointing to larger historical records of his deeds.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the reign of Josiah in Judah and is linked to the religious reforms already mentioned in the book. The notes point out that the order of the priests and Levites echoes the instructions of David and Solomon, and that the ark had probably been removed from the temple during a period of previous apostasy. It is also noted that the Passover of Josiah gathered a very large number of participants and that its celebration stood out for the real generosity and the correct participation of priests and Levites.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes that true biblical reform is not only destruction of error, but restoration of worship according to the word of God. Josiah is portrayed as a zealous king who values holiness, order and obedience to the Mosaic law. At the same time, the text teaches that previous religious fidelity does not exempt the believer from relying on discernment and humility: Josiah, though pious, acts without meeting the warning given to him and suffers the consequences. The narrative combines grace and judgment: there is a national celebration marked by joy and provision, but also a tragic end that shows human fragility. The memory of Josiah is preserved not as moral perfection, but as a testimony of a reign deeply dedicated to the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The distribution of tasks between priests and Levites follows the standards of David and Solomon, and, because of the practical situation, Josiah maintains the practice of the Levites assisting in the sacrifice of the passover, as had already happened in the reign of Hezekiah.
The Passover is treated as the main feasts instituted in the ceremonial law, and the celebration of Josiah appears as one of the great recoveries of religion in its time.
What made this Passover singular, according to the observation cited, was the great liberality of Josiah by providing victims in excess of what other kings had offered.

questions: What does the organization of the Passover teach about the importance of obeying God with order, reverence and community cooperation?
How does the example of Josiah show that a godly life still requires discernment to hear warnings and not act on impulse?
How does the king's generosity point to a leadership that serves the people rather than just demanding of it?
study.practice: Examine your life of worship and service: are there areas in which devotion is present, but the order, obedience, and participation of others are missing? Reevaluate your practices in the light of Scripture, value the shared service in the church and learn from Josiah both the zeal for holiness and the danger of ignoring wise counsel. Also, remember that a good work does not replace the need to remain attentive to God's word to the end.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not safely identify all the historical details mentioned in the biblical text, so the study avoids speculation about dates, geography or out-of-the-chapter events. There is also an important interpretative observation in Tyndale: the lamentations by Josiah should not be confused with the biblical book of Lamentations; the text only states that such lamentations were preserved in a collection now lost. The phrase about the ark in v. 3 is presented as a possibility, not as absolute certainty.
